docs.title: How OuterSpace fits your cluster
docs.text:
OuterSpace runs as a worker in your self-managed Kubernetes cluster. The OS provides the host and container runtime; your cluster supplies networking, workload scheduling and the applications.

Your workloads       Agent tasks or model-serving containers
                     Kubernetes deployments, services and storage
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Your cluster         Separate control plane and Cilium add-ons
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OuterSpace worker    kubelet · containerd · Linux · systemd
                     Read-only system + persistent node state
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CPU alpha            AMD64 or ARM64 UEFI virtual machine

docs.title: A host that stays separate from your applications
docs.text:
The system root is read-only and protected by dm-verity. Install application libraries, tools and serving engines in your workload containers. The running host does not use in-place apt upgrades.

Both worker profiles use the same Core. Agent adds the host policy and I/O budgets needed by its restricted execution profile. Inference provides a worker for your model-serving deployments, with a larger default state partition. See the profile comparison to choose an image.

docs.title: What persists
docs.text:
Storage Holds Behavior System root OS and host services Read-only Node state (/var) Container storage, worker identity and logs Survives reboot; unencrypted in the alpha Agent workspace and scratch Files created by a task Temporary; discarded with the pod Application data and model weights Your workload's data Storage and backups are managed by your deployment

An enrolled worker retains its hostname and rotated Kubernetes identity after restart. Its original config drive is no longer needed. Persistent node state is not an application backup; keep important data externally.

docs.title: Joining and networking
docs.text:
A config drive supplies the cluster API address, CA and a short-lived bootstrap token. Kubelet enrolls the node and rotates its certificates. The cluster operator controls serving-certificate approval and workload policy.

The supplied Cilium configuration provides cluster networking, services and network policy. The Agent profile starts with default-deny ingress and egress; the operator must allow the flows a task needs.

docs.title: Container storage
docs.text:
Containerd stores the images used by workloads in node state. Kubelet reclaims unused images periodically using age and disk-pressure settings. Budget disk space for both image layers and your workloads.

Optional Dragonfly peer delivery is experimental in this alpha. It does not replace local image storage or manage model weights. End-to-end peer delivery, private-registry access control and fleet cache behavior are outside the evaluated scope.

docs.title: Replacing a node
docs.text:
The alpha uses a single system slot and has no authenticated updater or rollback mechanism. Plan to drain and recreate disposable evaluation nodes when changing the OS image. UEFI boot requires Secure Boot to be disabled.

Follow Get started to prepare a worker. For design rationale, see the architecture decisions.

docs.title: Is this an OS or a container image?
docs.text: OuterSpace is an operating-system disk image for Kubernetes workers. Your agent tasks and inference applications run in containers on that host. The OS has a read-only system root and separate persistent node state.

docs.title: Does it create a Kubernetes cluster for me?
docs.text: You provide a self-managed control plane and configure the worker to join it. The alpha uses Kubernetes 1.36 with the supplied Cilium configuration. It is not a supported replacement for a managed cloud provider's node image.

docs.title: Which profile should I choose?
docs.text: Choose Agent for small containerized tasks that fit the supplied execution policy and resource budgets. Choose Inference to host CPU model-serving containers. Both are available for AMD64 and ARM64; see the profile comparison.

docs.title: Does OuterSpace include an agent framework or a model?
docs.text: You deploy those separately. The Agent profile supplies the execution boundary for task containers; it does not manage agent reasoning, credentials or approvals. The Inference alpha has been exercised with llama.cpp, but the serving engine and model weights are not bundled into the OS.

docs.title: What survives a restart?
docs.text: The worker's identity, container storage and logs live in persistent state. Agent task workspaces are temporary and disappear when their pods are removed. Keep important application data externally. The alpha does not encrypt the state partition or provide an authenticated update/rollback path.

docs.title: Can I use a GPU or install it on a server?
docs.text: Evaluate this release in disposable UEFI VMs with Secure Boot disabled. GPU support and a qualified bare-metal hardware matrix are not available yet.

docs.title: Is it ready for production?
docs.text: It is an experimental CPU alpha, without a production support commitment or performance guarantee. Review the release limits and security scope, including the time-limited kernel risk acceptance.

docs.title: Where do I download it?
docs.text: The alpha release is still a draft. Public downloads will appear on GitHub Releases after publication. Follow Get started to build the tagged source in the meantime.

docs.title: Choose your worker
docs.text:
OuterSpace OS has two profiles built on the same immutable Ubuntu-based Core. Choose a profile for each worker according to the workloads it will host. Both CPU profiles target AMD64 and ARM64.

Agent Inference Intended use Small, containerized agent tasks and tools CPU model-serving containers Workload policy Restricted execution with fixed budgets and default-deny networking Your Kubernetes deployment and resource policy Application stack Bring your task containers and external orchestration Bring your serving engine and model weights Default persistent state 2 GiB 8 GiB

docs.title: Agent: give each task a boundary
docs.text:
Use the Agent profile to execute tasks under policies owned by the cluster operator. The supplied profile requires an unprivileged container, a read-only container root, AppArmor and seccomp. It rejects privileged execution, host mounts, runtime sockets and injected credentials. Network access is denied until the operator explicitly permits a flow.

The first alpha supports one container per task, with ceilings of 1 CPU and 256 MiB RAM. Each task has a temporary 64 MiB workspace and 16 MiB scratch area. Process and disk-I/O limits bound resource use; log rotation limits retained logs. Workspaces are discarded with the task. The supplied namespace allows four active tasks, including queued launches.

This profile suits small tools and bounded jobs. A larger agent framework or model server needs a different deployment arrangement. The alpha does not provide an agent framework, credential broker or approval service. Tasks share the host kernel within one trusted administrative domain; this is not VM isolation for mutually untrusted tenants.

See the Agent configuration and example workload to apply the profile and adapt a task container.

docs.title: Inference: keep model serving in your workloads
docs.text:
Use the Inference profile for a Kubernetes worker dedicated to CPU model serving. Your serving engine and weights live outside the host image, so changing a model or application does not require baking it into the OS.

The alpha supports CPU serving, workload replacement, node draining and recovery after a worker restart. It has been exercised with llama.cpp. Choose models that fit the memory and compute resources of your evaluation VM; the alpha makes no throughput or latency guarantee.

GPU acceleration is not available in this release. Model storage, application availability and the licenses of your model and serving engine remain part of your workload deployment.

docs.title: Shared host behavior
docs.text:
Both profiles provide a read-only system root, persistent container and node state, Kubernetes certificate rotation, and networking through the supplied Cilium configuration. Persistent state is unencrypted. Neither profile includes the Kubernetes control plane.

Get started with a disposable CPU VM and review the alpha limits before deploying a workload.

docs.title: Try OuterSpace OS
docs.text: Start with a disposable CPU virtual machine in a self-managed Kubernetes cluster. Choose Agent for small, bounded task containers or Inference for CPU model serving. Read the profile comparison and alpha limits before preparing a worker.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A UEFI VM matching your image architecture, with 4 vCPUs and 4 GiB RAM and Secure Boot disabled. This is the reference setup, not a model-sizing guide.
  • A separate Kubernetes 1.36 control plane reachable from the worker, with TLS bootstrap and certificate rotation enabled.
  • Cilium 1.20.3, deployed using the supplied cluster configuration. Use a dedicated evaluation cluster; do not replace an existing cluster's CNI using these instructions.
  • The control plane CA, a dedicated short-lived bootstrap token and your cluster DNS address.

The worker image does not create the control plane. Application containers, serving engines and model weights are deployed separately.

docs.title: Prepare an image
docs.text:
0.1.0-alpha.1 is currently a draft release. Public downloads will appear on GitHub Releases when published. You can build the tagged source now.

Install Python 3.11+, Make and Docker running Linux containers. The build uses Docker's native architecture: ARM64 on Apple Silicon, AMD64 on x86 hosts. Allow disk space for the image, source archives and reusable download caches.

git clone https://github.com/Alien6-Studio/outerspace-os.git
cd outerspace-os
git checkout v0.1.0-alpha.1
make PROFILE=agent HARDWARE=cpu builder build smoke package
# Use PROFILE=inference for a model-serving worker.

Images and bundles are written under out/<profile>-cpu-<architecture>/. The command also boots the image to check that it starts successfully. See the build guide for output files and options.

docs.title: Verify a release bundle
docs.text:
When downloads are available, choose the archive matching your profile and architecture. Download its .sha256 and .tar.attestation.jsonl companions, plus verify-attestation.py and its checksum. Check the archive and helper checksums, then extract the archive into a new directory.

With Python 3.11+ and the GitHub CLI installed, authenticate the bundle's inner SHA256SUMS inventory using the supplied helper. Replace the two paths below; the expected source, tag and build run are fixed for this alpha:

python3 verify-attestation.py \
  --checksums /path/to/extracted/SHA256SUMS \
  --bundle /path/to/archive.tar.attestation.jsonl \
  --commit a1df243a099e8ab74ba2c1706a0fa719d681c689 \
  --tag v0.1.0-alpha.1 \
  --run 41219970340

Inside the extracted bundle, run sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS before decompressing or using the raw disk. On macOS, use shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS. The attestation authenticates the inventory; it does not enable Secure Boot.

docs.title: Connect the worker to your cluster
docs.text:
From the matching source checkout, generate a config drive with your cluster's values. Store the bootstrap token in a protected file:

python3 build/tools/node-config.py \
  --api-server https://api.example.net:6443 \
  --ca /secure/cluster-ca.crt \
  --token-file /secure/bootstrap-token \
  --cluster-dns 10.96.0.10
make config-drive

Use the raw OS image as the VM's boot disk and attach out/node-config.raw as a second disk. Boot through UEFI with Secure Boot disabled. Check the worker from your evaluation cluster's Kubernetes context:

kubectl get nodes -o wide

The control plane must have an explicit approval policy for serving-certificate requests. Once the node has enrolled, detach the config drive and revoke the bootstrap token. The drive contains credentials: keep it private. The worker retains its rotated identity in persistent state and can boot without the drive.

Manage workloads through Kubernetes. The image has locked local accounts and no SSH server or shared password.

docs.title: Deploy your workload
docs.text:
For Agent, apply the supplied execution profile, label the intended worker and adapt the example task container using the Agent setup instructions. Network access is denied by default; allow only the flows your task needs.

For Inference, deploy your CPU serving container and model weights through Kubernetes, selecting the OuterSpace worker and setting suitable resource requests and limits. Keep important model and application data externally.

See the worker configuration reference for cluster integration details. If enrollment or a workload fails, report the version, profile, architecture and reproduction steps in an issue, without credentials.

docs.title: A dedicated host for AI workers
docs.text: OuterSpace OS is an immutable, Ubuntu-based Linux distribution for Kubernetes workers running agent tasks and inference. It brings the host system, container runtime and node services together in one image. Your tools, serving engines and models stay in containers, where you can deploy and replace them independently.

docs.title: Where it fits
docs.text:
Use OuterSpace when you operate a self-managed Kubernetes cluster and want dedicated workers for AI workloads. The OS supplies Linux, systemd, containerd and kubelet. You supply the control plane, Cilium networking and the applications you want to run.

The system root is read-only. Container storage, logs and the worker's identity live in separate persistent state, so an enrolled node can restart and rejoin the cluster without its original bootstrap credentials.

docs.title: Pick a profile
docs.text:
Agent provides bounded execution for small containerized tasks and tools. The operator controls admission and network access; each task runs with restricted permissions and fixed resource budgets.

Inference hosts CPU model-serving containers. Deploy your serving engine and weights through Kubernetes, replace the workload as it changes, and drain the worker when you need to take it out of service.

Both profiles are available as source builds for AMD64 and ARM64. The profile guide explains the differences and the Agent alpha's limits.

docs.title: Start with a disposable VM
docs.text:
The current version, 0.1.0-alpha.1, is a CPU preview. Its release is still a draft, so public downloads are pending. Build the tagged source to evaluate it today, using a UEFI VM with 4 vCPUs, 4 GiB RAM and Secure Boot disabled.

GPU workers, bare-metal support and production operation are outside this alpha. Read the release information, then follow Get started.

docs.title: 0.1.0-alpha.1 — AI workers on CPU
docs.text:
The first OuterSpace OS alpha lets you evaluate a dedicated Kubernetes worker OS for agent tasks and model serving. It is intended for teams exploring these workloads in a self-managed cluster, using disposable CPU virtual machines.

The release is currently a draft. Public downloads will appear on GitHub Releases when published. You can build the tagged source today.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Run bounded agent tasks. The Agent profile combines restricted container execution, default-deny networking and enforced resource budgets for small tasks and tools controlled by your operator.
  • Serve models on CPU. The Inference profile hosts your containerized serving engine and weights. Deploy a model, replace the workload, drain the node and recover after a worker restart. The alpha has been exercised with llama.cpp.
  • Keep the host separate from your applications. Both profiles use a read-only system root and persistent node state. An enrolled worker retains its identity across restarts.

Agent and Inference each have AMD64 and ARM64 images. Your Kubernetes control plane, cluster add-ons, application containers and model weights are deployed separately. See Choose your worker for profile details.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Use a UEFI VM with 4 vCPUs and 4 GiB RAM, with Secure Boot disabled, and a separate Kubernetes 1.36 control plane with the supplied Cilium configuration. Choose a profile, prepare the image and configure the worker to join your cluster.

The getting-started guide covers building an image, verifying a downloaded bundle and enrolling the worker. Release bundles include checksums, attestations, a software inventory, sources and license notices.

docs.title: Know the limits
docs.text:
This is an evaluation preview, with no production support commitment or performance guarantee. GPU workers, a qualified bare-metal hardware matrix, Secure Boot and authenticated update/rollback are not available. Persistent state is unencrypted; keep important data externally.

Agent tasks share the host kernel. The alpha does not provide a credential broker, approval service or isolation for mutually untrusted tenants.

The accepted CVE-2019-14899 risk applies only to the stock CPU configuration without host VPNs or custom networking and expires on 14 November 2026 at 06:24:43 UTC. See the security scope for the exact boundary.

docs.title: Share your experience
docs.text: Report a problem with your version, profile, architecture and the steps that reproduce it. Evaluation support is best-effort. Report vulnerabilities through the private security channel.

docs.title: Security for the CPU alpha
docs.text: OuterSpace separates the read-only host system from writable node state. The Agent profile adds restricted execution and resource budgets for task containers. Use the alpha in a disposable evaluation environment under one trusted administrative domain.

docs.title: Host and workload protections
docs.text:
• Read-only root. dm-verity detects corruption of the system filesystem. It does not authenticate the boot chain; Secure Boot must be disabled for this alpha.
  • Restricted Agent tasks. The supplied profile requires AppArmor, seccomp and unprivileged execution. It refuses host access and privilege escalation, and enforces resource budgets. Network access is denied unless the operator explicitly permits it.
  • Worker identity. Kubernetes enrollment uses a short-lived bootstrap token and certificate rotation. The enrolled worker keeps its identity after reboot.
  • Verifiable downloads. Release bundles include checksums, GitHub attestations, a software inventory, corresponding sources and original license notices. Follow the verification steps before using a downloaded image.

docs.title: Boundaries to understand
docs.text:
Agent tasks share the host kernel. This alpha is not intended to isolate mutually untrusted tenants and supplies no credential broker or approval service.

Persistent node state is unencrypted. There is no authenticated A/B updater or rollback mechanism. Keep important data externally and plan to recreate evaluation nodes. The release has no CIS certification, production support commitment or qualified GPU/bare-metal hardware matrix.

Optional Dragonfly peer delivery remains experimental. Private-image access control, peer security and fleet cache behavior are outside the evaluated alpha scope; do not use it to share private images across tenants.

docs.title: Time-limited kernel risk
docs.text:
CVE-2019-14899 is accepted only for the stock CPU alpha until 14 November 2026, 06:24:43 UTC. That scope excludes host VPN clients, configured VPN tunnels and custom network configurations. IPsec/XFRM remains compiled for Cilium; no universal kernel fix is claimed.

The acceptance is conditional on the reviewed image and configuration. It does not extend to a modified image or beyond its expiry date. The release bundles retain the vulnerability reports and recorded review decisions.

docs.title: Report a vulnerability
docs.text: Use the private security advisory channel. Include the version, profile, architecture and steps needed to reproduce the problem. See the security policy for reporting details.
